question: Crew Resource Management (CRM) is best defined as:

options.text: A training programme concerned exclusively with manual flying skill
The effective use of all available resources — human, informational and equipment — to achieve a safe and efficient flight
A set of rules concerned only with how pilots should greet each other
A term that applies only to single-pilot operations, where the one pilot must use every resource alone without any help from other people in the cockpit

explanation: CRM grew out of the recognition that accidents were increasingly caused not by a lack of technical flying skill but by a failure to use the resources actually available — each other, the aircraft's systems, ATC, documentation — as well as possible.

question: CRM training developed in response to the recognition that:

options.text: Pilots of the era lacked basic flying skill at the controls, which meant that most accidents could be traced to a simple lack of hands-on competence in the cockpit
A significant number of accidents involved technically proficient crews who nonetheless failed at communication, leadership or decision making
CRM has no connection to any real accident history
Aircraft systems were fundamentally too unreliable to fly safely

explanation: A number of well-studied accidents involved crews with perfectly adequate technical skill, where the breakdown was instead in communication, leadership, workload management or decision making — exactly the gap CRM training was developed to close.

question: CRM treats effective teamwork and communication as:

options.text: A fixed personality trait that cannot be trained or improved
A topic that needs no ongoing practice once covered once, because a single course is enough to fix the skill permanently in the memory of the crew
Relevant only to the captain, never to other crew members
A skill that can and should be deliberately trained and practised, not simply an innate trait some people have and others lack

explanation: CRM's premise is that teamwork, communication and leadership are learnable, trainable skills, just like a stick-and-rudder skill — which is why they are practised, assessed and refreshed through recurrent training rather than being treated as a fixed trait a person either has or does not.

question: The distinction CRM training draws between "hearing" and "listening" is that listening additionally involves:

options.text: Exactly the same process as hearing, with no meaningful difference
Only applying to written communication, never to spoken words, because listening is a skill used when reading messages rather than during speech
Only applying to written communication, never to spoken words
Actively processing and understanding the meaning of what is said, not simply registering the sound of it

explanation: Hearing is the passive physical reception of sound; listening is the active process of attending to and genuinely understanding what is being communicated — a crew member can hear a radio call perfectly well while still failing to actually listen to what it meant.

question: A crew member recognising that they are becoming overloaded should, as a CRM practice, generally:

options.text: Say nothing and attempt to push through every task alone
Wait until a task is missed before mentioning any difficulty
Communicate it to the other crew member and actively shed or delegate lower-priority tasks
Take on additional tasks to prove they can cope, since accepting every extra job shows the crew that the individual is competent and reliable under pressure

explanation: Overload is far easier to manage once it is shared: openly acknowledging it lets the other crew member redistribute tasks or take over something lower priority, rather than discovering the overload only after something has already been missed.

question: When workload becomes very high, an established CRM-consistent priority for a crew to protect above almost everything else is:

options.text: Responding immediately to every radio call, regardless of its relevance to the immediate situation
Completing every secondary administrative task, even at the expense of basic aircraft control
There is no agreed priority; all tasks are treated as equally important at all times, so the crew simply works through each one in the order received
Basic aircraft control and navigation ("fly the aircraft first"), with secondary tasks shed or deferred as needed

explanation: The long-standing "aviate, navigate, communicate" priority exists precisely for moments of overload: when everything cannot be done at once, basic control and navigation of the aircraft take priority, and everything else is shed or delayed until capacity allows.

question: A core CRM goal around situational awareness is to ensure that:

options.text: Only the captain needs an accurate picture of the situation, since the captain alone is responsible for every decision the crew makes in flight
Situational awareness is relevant only to single-pilot operations
Both crew members maintain a shared, accurate understanding of the situation, rather than each privately holding a different picture
Each crew member's mental model is kept entirely private and never discussed

explanation: Two crew members who privately hold different pictures of the situation cannot effectively monitor or support each other. CRM emphasises actively building and checking a shared understanding, not assuming it will naturally stay aligned on its own.

question: Confidential (or anonymous) incident reporting systems exist in aviation mainly to:

options.text: Apply only to air traffic controllers, never to pilots, since flight crew are assumed to be trained well enough that their errors do not need to be recorded at all
Apply only to air traffic controllers, never to pilots
Allow regulators to assign individual blame more easily
Encourage honest reporting of errors and near-misses by removing the fear of personal blame, so the industry can learn from them before they become accidents

explanation: The central insight behind confidential reporting is that far more can be learned from the many near-misses and minor errors that never become accidents than from the rare accident itself — but only if people feel safe enough to report them honestly.

question: The idea that most accidents are preceded by a larger number of minor incidents and near-misses sharing similar underlying causes supports the view that:

options.text: Only the accident itself is worth investigating, since minor incidents have no bearing on how a later accident should be explained or prevented
Studying and acting on minor incidents can help prevent the larger accident they are warning signs of
Near-misses occur at a completely random rate with no pattern
Minor incidents have no relationship to accidents and can be safely ignored

explanation: If accidents and the near-misses that precede them tend to share underlying causes, then addressing the causes behind the frequent minor events is a proactive way to reduce the rare but serious accidents — which is the whole rationale for taking incident reporting seriously rather than waiting for an actual accident to learn the same lesson.

question: Fear of personal blame or disciplinary action is widely recognised as:

options.text: Something that only affects reporting of deliberate violations, never honest mistakes
A major barrier to honest incident reporting, which a genuine just culture is specifically designed to reduce
Entirely eliminated once a reporting system simply exists on paper
A factor with no bearing on whether people choose to file a report, since staff always report every error they make regardless of the consequences

explanation: A reporting system that exists on paper does not guarantee honest reports if people still fear personal consequences for reporting their own error. This is exactly why a genuine just culture — distinguishing honest mistakes from reckless or deliberate violations — matters as much as the reporting system itself.

question: An effective incident reporting scheme depends on which of the following to actually produce safety improvements over time?

options.text: The volume of reports filed each year, regardless of what is done with them
Reports being collected, analysed, and genuinely acted upon, rather than merely filed away
Reports being collected and then never reviewed by anyone, since the filing itself is considered sufficient to show that the organisation takes safety seriously
Only the most dramatic reports, with minor ones automatically discarded

explanation: This mirrors the "learning culture" idea described elsewhere in this subject: a reporting scheme only translates into real safety improvement if the information collected is actually analysed and acted on, not merely gathered for its own sake.

question: Using all available resources, in the CRM sense, explicitly includes drawing on:

options.text: Only the captain's input, excluding any other crew member, because the captain is always best placed to judge every resource that is available
Only the handling pilot's own memory and judgement, with nothing else considered a resource
Other crew members, ATC, ground staff, written procedures and the aircraft's own systems, not only the handling pilot's own judgement
Only equipment, with people excluded from the definition of a resource

explanation: CRM deliberately widens what counts as a usable resource well beyond one person's own judgement — the rest of the crew, ATC, ground support, documentation and the aircraft's systems are all resources that, used well, improve the quality of the overall response.

question: CRM training places particular emphasis on how instructions and concerns are phrased mainly because:

options.text: Vague, indirect phrasing can be misunderstood or underweighted, especially across an authority gradient, in a way that clear, direct phrasing avoids
Phrasing has no measurable effect on how a message is received
Only the words used matter, with no role for tone or timing
Only the words used matter, with no role for tone or timing, since a precise choice of words on its own is always enough to ensure that any instruction is followed in full

explanation: This connects directly to the metacommunication and assertiveness points raised elsewhere in this subject: CRM trains clear, unambiguous phrasing — especially for raising a safety concern — precisely because softer, indirect wording is more easily missed or discounted, particularly by someone senior who is not actively listening for it.

question: CRM training on decision making tends to emphasise that the best decisions on the flight deck usually come from:

options.text: Combining and cross-checking the crew's shared information and judgement, rather than one person deciding entirely alone whenever time allows for the discussion
A decision being made with no reference to information from any other crew member in every situation, since the quickest decisions are those taken alone without discussion
A decision being made with no reference to information from any other crew member
The most senior crew member always deciding alone with no input from anyone else, regardless of time available

explanation: This builds directly on the leadership-style material elsewhere in this subject: where time allows, drawing on the full crew's combined information and judgement generally produces a better-informed decision than relying on one person's view alone, even if that person is the most senior.

question: CRM training often distinguishes between assertive, aggressive and passive styles of raising a concern. An assertive style is generally the recommended one because it:

options.text: Means raising every concern as forcefully and confrontationally as possible
Has no meaningful difference from either a passive or an aggressive style
States the concern clearly and directly while still remaining respectful, rather than either staying silent (passive) or becoming confrontational (aggressive)
Has no meaningful difference from either a passive or an aggressive style, since all three ways of raising a concern lead to exactly the same outcome in practice, whatever the situation

explanation: Assertiveness sits deliberately between the two less effective extremes: it gets the concern across clearly and is far more likely to actually be heard and acted on than a passive, hedged remark, without the relationship damage or defensive reaction an aggressive, confrontational approach tends to provoke.

question: CRM skills, like a manual flying skill, are generally found to:

options.text: Remain permanently at their initial level once learned, with no need for refreshment
Decay without ongoing practice, which is why CRM is covered in recurrent training rather than being taught only once
Have no connection to deliberate practice of any kind, since these skills are considered innate and develop with no training regardless of what is done
Improve automatically over time with no further training required

explanation: Treating CRM as a genuine skill means accepting it behaves like one — it can fade without use — which is exactly why it is built into recurrent training rather than delivered once during initial licensing and never revisited.

question: Aeronautical Information Circulars and comparable published safety bulletins serve a function related to incident reporting by:

options.text: Being relevant only to air traffic control, never to flight crew, because bulletins are written for controllers and not for the people flying the aircraft
Being relevant only to air traffic control, never to flight crew
Containing no information connected to human factors or safety
Disseminating lessons learned from past incidents and accidents to the wider aviation community, beyond the specific operator or location involved

explanation: An incident reported and analysed in one place does little good if the lesson stays there; published safety circulars and bulletins are one of the ways a specific finding gets shared with the much wider community that could just as easily encounter the same hazard.

question: A crew member who stays silent about a genuine safety concern specifically to avoid an uncomfortable confrontation is displaying:

options.text: A style with no connection to flight safety
The ideal response in every circumstance, since staying quiet is always the most polite and professional way to handle any concern on the flight deck
A passive communication style, which risks the concern never being raised at all
The ideal response in every circumstance

explanation: Passive communication avoids the short-term discomfort of speaking up, but at the cost of the concern potentially never being heard at all — precisely the failure mode CRM training's emphasis on assertiveness is meant to counter.

question: CRM principles are generally considered to apply:

options.text: Only to captains, never to first officers or cabin crew
Across the whole operation — flight crew, cabin crew, dispatch, maintenance and air traffic control — not to pilots alone
Only to the two pilots on the flight deck
Only during an actual declared emergency, since the everyday operation of the aircraft is outside the scope of any crew resource management principle at all

explanation: Because safety depends on how well the whole operation coordinates, not just the two people on the flight deck, CRM-style training has broadened over time to cover cabin crew, dispatchers, maintenance personnel and controllers as well as pilots.

question: The overall purpose that CRM training and confidential incident reporting share, tying this topic back to the opening topic of this subject, is:

options.text: Assigning individual blame as efficiently as possible after an accident has already occurred
Reducing operating costs, with safety being only a secondary, unintended effect
Strengthening the organization's defences against error before it combines into an accident, in the spirit of Reason's Swiss Cheese model
Two entirely unrelated programmes with no common purpose, kept separate so that each department can manage its own budget and reporting without interference

explanation: Both CRM and honest incident reporting are, at bottom, ways of strengthening the organization's layered defences — better teamwork and communication close gaps before they open, and reporting surfaces gaps that have opened so they can be closed — the same underlying logic the Swiss Cheese model gives for why accidents happen in the first place.
